0.text: A service in a TurboTax-style filing product that shows customers where their most recent tax refund is, from the moment their return is filed until the money arrives, and predicts how long the rest of the wait will take.

1.text: Once a customer files their federal and state returns, the refund disappears into a process they can't see. The IRS and state tax agencies receive the return, validate it, possibly flag it for review, approve it, and finally pay it out, sometimes for a different amount than was claimed. Those agencies update on their own schedules, often with delays, and none of their systems were built to answer the two questions the customer has: "Where is my refund, and when will I get it?" Answering the second question takes more than relaying the agency's status. Until an agency sets a payment date, the service uses an AI model to estimate when the refund will be available. The model is trained on how long similar returns actually took, so the system also has to collect that training data and make inference requests, all without exposing taxpayer data. Without a reliable way to answer those questions themselves, taxpayers call support lines, file duplicate returns, or simply worry. Support centers are overwhelmed in exactly the weeks when they're needed most, and the people waiting on the refund, often counting on it to pay bills, get vague answers. Design a service that gives customers an accurate, timely, and secure view of the status of their most recent refund, predicts when a refund that hasn't arrived will be available, tells them what to do if there's a problem, and stays available under the extreme, seasonal load of filing season.

2.text: Taxpayers Customers who filed through the product and are signed in to their account. Most check a handful of times; some check daily. They use phones more than desktops. Support agents Call-center staff who need the same status view the taxpayer sees, so their answers match what the taxpayer read online. Operations and data science Engineers who run the agency integrations through peak season, and the team that trains, evaluates, and monitors the refund-time model.

3.section: Where it fits in the journey
3.text: The service begins after filing is complete. It does not prepare or submit returns; it observes the refund as it moves through processing. Return received The agency has the return. The model gives a first estimate of when the refund will arrive. Under processing Validation, matching, and any manual review. The estimate is refreshed as the return moves; if the agency needs something, the customer is told what to do. Refund approved The agency confirms the amount and sets a payment date, which replaces the estimate. Refund sent Funds are released by direct deposit or check, either as filed or, if the agency changed the amount, as a refund adjusted with the reason.

4.text: Seasonal, spiky traffic. Load is concentrated in a few months a year, with sharp peaks around the start of the season, filing deadlines, and the days payments go out. The system must handle many times its average load without degrading. Sensitive data behind one sign-in. A customer's account holds tax IDs, income, and bank details, so account takeover is the main threat. Sign-in has to be strong without being painful, and nothing about one customer's refund may leak to another. Status comes from systems we don't control. The IRS and each state own the truth, update on different schedules, and offer no push notifications, so the service has to ask them, in bulk, within their rate limits. Predicting an uncertain wait. Processing times vary with the filing date, the credits claimed, the agency's backlog, and review. The estimate has to be honest about its uncertainty, fall back gracefully when the model is unavailable, and train on outcomes without exposing personal data. Accuracy over freshness, but not too stale. Showing the wrong status is worse than showing a slightly old one. Updates every few hours may be acceptable; a contradictory answer is not. Reducing, not shifting, support load. A vague status ("still processing") just moves the phone call later. The status must be specific enough to set expectations.

5.text: Show the current status of a customer's most recent federal and state refunds for the current tax year. Until the agency sets a payment date, show an AI estimate of when the refund will be available, as a range. Show the agency's payment date and amount once known, including why a refund was adjusted. Tell customers what to do when there's a problem: the agency needs information, the refund changed, or it's late. Protect accounts with strong sign-in, and resist takeover, enumeration, and abuse. Collect training data and serve predictions without exposing personal data. Stay available and fast during peak filing season. Optionally notify taxpayers when their status changes, so they don't need to keep checking.

6.text: Preparing, filing, or amending tax returns. Changing refund details such as the amount or bank account. Guaranteeing a payment date. The estimate is a prediction; only the agency sets the date. Showing prior tax years, or paying a balance due. Returns with no refund show the balance the agency reports, and payment happens elsewhere. Replacing the agencies' processing systems, which own the status.

9.text: What this design takes as given. Each assumption has its basis and what would change if it's wrong, so the riskiest ones can be checked first. The riskiest assumption is the agency status feed. Everything else can be adjusted with configuration or capacity. If no agency will provide a bulk feed to partners, the status source changes, not just its size.

10.text: Assumption Basis If it's wrong Only the most recent tax year is shown The problem statement asks for the most recent refund Prior years need longer retention and amended-return statuses. One federal return, plus one return for each state with an income tax that the taxpayer lived or worked in, with at most one full resident state A person has one home state at a time. Movers file part-year returns in both states, and commuters file nonresident returns where they work Supported in the demo. Joint filers who live in different states, and cities with their own income tax, aren't modeled. States with no income tax on wages need no return, whether the taxpayer lives there, worked there, or both Nine states don't tax wages: Alaska, Florida, Nevada, New Hampshire, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Washington, and Wyoming. The demo models Florida, Texas, and Washington A state that starts taxing wages needs a form, tax math, and an agency adapter. Washington's capital gains tax is a reminder that "no income tax" can have exceptions. Where a taxpayer lives and works is recorded even when no state return results It explains an empty state section to the taxpayer, and to support agents who see the same view Without it, a Texas resident with only a federal return looks like a filer whose state return is missing. A taxpayer living in a state with no income tax gets no credit on a nonresident return elsewhere The credit for tax paid to other states is claimed on a resident return, and there isn't one None in the demo: the nonresident return already taxes only that state's share of income. The resident state's credit for tax paid to other states is limited to its own tax on that income How California and New York both work, simplified: the demo applies the limit to the whole credit, not income type by income type Real credits have more rules (which income qualifies, which states have reciprocity), so the demo's refund can differ from a real return. The filing product transmits returns; this service observes them afterwards Filing is a separate product. The demo includes a processor only to stand in for it If this service owns transmission, the submission queue becomes a core component. Nothing here can change a refund amount or bank account Read-only toward money is a security principle Any write path to money needs dual control and much stronger review.

11.text: Assumption Basis If it's wrong About 40 million customers in a season The scale of a large consumer tax product The design scales out, but capacity and cost estimates change in proportion. About 90% of filings arrive between late January and April 15, with a smaller rush before October 15 IRS filing-season statistics for 2024–2026 A flatter season lowers peak cost. A sharper one needs more headroom. Each customer checks about 8 times a season, mostly on phones Several checks per return, more while waiting for money Many more checks shift the bottleneck to the read path and caching.

12.text: Assumption Basis If it's wrong Agencies offer a bulk status feed to e-file partners No agency offers one today: refund status after acceptance is only available to taxpayers themselves. This is the riskiest assumption. Without a feed, status falls back to e-file acknowledgments plus the model's estimate, or to taxpayer-authorized lookups. Agencies never push updates; we have to ask Agencies offer no push notifications today If they push, batch polling becomes reconciliation, and status gets fresher. Each agency has its own rate limit, schedule, and credentials Each agency runs its own systems Shared infrastructure would simplify the adapters, not remove them. Updates every few hours are acceptable Agencies update in daily or nightly cycles; showing the wrong status is worse than an old one If minutes matter, polling cost rises sharply, and only a push feed makes it affordable. Agencies are slow or unavailable at peak Peak load hits agencies at the same time it hits us If agencies keep up, the queues and circuit breakers are rarely used, but they cost little.

13.text: Assumption Basis If it's wrong We never need full tax IDs or bank account numbers to show status The last 4 digits, plus a keyed fingerprint for fraud checks, are enough Storing full identifiers would need tokenization and a much stricter data boundary. Return information is covered by §7216, so model training needs separate opt-in consent IRC §7216 and its regulations If too few taxpayers opt in, the model falls back to published agency guidance more often. Taxpayers accept a range, not a date, until the agency sets one Only the agency can promise a payment date A single date would be wrong more often, and would create calls instead of preventing them.

14.text: Assumption Basis If it's wrong Kubernetes and managed Postgres are available, in more than one availability zone Standard platform for a product at this scale Without them, failover and scaling have to be built rather than configured. One team owns the service, with on-call through filing season The service is critical for a few months a year Without dedicated on-call, peak-season readiness and game days carry more risk.

26.section: Decision: answer from our own data
26.text: A read could call the agency live, which sounds fresher. We don't, because agencies are slow, rate limited, and sometimes down, exactly when traffic peaks. Instead, the batch sync keeps our copy current, and the page says how recent it is. A status can be a little old, which we show honestly. It can't be wrong, and the page can't go down because an agency did.

29.section: Decision: a signed-in account, not an SSN lookup
29.text: The IRS's Where's My Refund asks for an SSN, a filing status, and the exact refund amount, because it has to work for anyone without signing in. We don't: the customer filed through our product. Sign-in replaces facts that identity thieves can buy, and it means the service never accepts a tax ID from anyone. The cost is one more sign-in, which passkeys and remembered devices keep short. Demo marks requirements the demo meets today. Planned marks what production adds.

47.text: Taxpayers read their status far more often than anything is written, and they read it hardest in the weeks when every other system is busiest. The service has to answer through all of it. When availability and latency pull against each other, availability wins: a slower answer, or an older one that says how old it is, beats an error. 99.95% status reads available in season < 300 ms p99 status read 0 read outage from losing a zone 0 committed filings lost Someone who asks where their refund is always gets an answer: the current status if we have it, the last one we know with its age if we don't. Never someone else's, and never a contradictory one.

48.text: Never wrong. A status that's old and says so isn't wrong. Another taxpayer's status, or one that contradicts what the agency told them, is. Always answer. Spend latency, money, and freshness to keep answering. Answer fast. Inside the first two, as fast as we can. Freshness gives way to availability because agency data is already hours old: the IRS updates refund status about once a day. A read a few seconds behind the primary changes nothing a taxpayer can see. See Assumptions .

Status reads ~280 a second, bursts to ~1,000 No Filings ~100 a second in the busiest hour Yes Status changes from agencies ~400 a second during a batch run Yes, from background workers only Reads don't need the writable database, so they shouldn't depend on it. Replicas answer them, and a cache can answer them when no database can. Reads are cheap: one indexed lookup, a few milliseconds. One replica could carry the whole peak. 51.text: Good: any answer within 2 seconds, including the taxpayer's own mistakes: a wrong password, an expired session, a return that doesn't exist. Bad: server errors, timeouts, anything slower than 2 seconds, and requests we turn away to shed load. Past 2 seconds, people refresh, so a slow answer is as good as no answer. Degraded: an answer from a fallback, such as the status cache, counts as good, so the objective isn't spent when the design works. Degraded answers are counted separately, and more than 1% for 15 minutes opens an incident, so fallbacks can't hide a real outage. Measured from outside too. Synthetic checks from several regions sign in and read a status every minute, catching DNS, edge, and certificate failures that internal metrics miss.

52.text: The two objectives are enforced differently, on purpose: Availability Latency Alert Pages when the budget burns fast: 2% of the month's in an hour, or 5% in six hours Opens a ticket when p99 is over 300 ms for 30 minutes. 55.text: Extending a session's expiry on every signed-in request would make every status read a write: a primary failover would take reads down with it, and the busiest table in a read-heavy service would be sessions . So checking a session only reads: Demo A session is extended at most once every 5 minutes, in the background. If that write fails, the request still succeeds. Idle timeouts stay accurate to within 5 minutes. Demo If the database can't confirm a session, the request is rejected with a 503, and the cookie is kept for when it can. This is the one place we choose security over availability. Planned Check sessions in the status cache, falling back to a replica. Planned Signing out and account locks write to the primary and remove the session from the cache at once.

56.text: Replicas trail the primary by up to a second. Right after filing, the dashboard could briefly miss the new return, which is exactly the kind of moment that leads to a duplicate filing. So: Planned The submit response includes the saved return, and the portal shows it straight away. Planned For 30 seconds after a taxpayer's own write, their reads go to the primary. If the primary is down, they go to a replica as usual.

57.text: Step Normally Timeout On timeout Check the session (cache) ~1 ms 50 ms Check it on a replica Read statuses (zone replica) 2–10 ms 150 ms Retry once on another zone's replica, then the primary Read statuses (primary) Only on fallback 300 ms Answer from the status cache, with its age Whole request p99 under 300 ms 2 s deadline Return 503; the portal retries once and keeps showing the last status Retries are budgeted. At most 10% of a pod's requests may be retries, and a replica that times out is skipped for 30 seconds. A slow database gets less traffic, not a retry storm. The portal retries once, after 0.5 to 1.5 seconds of jitter, so a failed zone doesn't turn into a synchronized wave of refreshes. If that fails, it keeps showing the last status it loaded.

60.text: Freshness: reads may trail the primary by a second, and fallbacks by minutes. Every answer shows its age. Write latency: waiting for the standby in another zone adds a few milliseconds to every commit. Money: three zones running at two-thirds, and a cache we don't need for speed. Complexity: two places a status can come from. The cache is written only after the database commits and read only when the database can't answer, so it can lag but never contradict.

61.text: A regional outage becomes a credible risk, or the target rises past 99.95%. Being read-heavy makes a second region cheap: an async replica and cache there can serve status reads read-only while filing waits for the home region. An agency offers push updates. Freshness would then be minutes, and the read-your-own-writes window and cache refresh would need tightening to match. Reads stop being cheap, for example if live predictions move onto the read path. Then the cache would also be needed for latency, and the timeouts above would need a new budget.

70.section: What this means for the design
70.text: Serve every status read from our own data. Agency latency and outages never reach customers. Poll agencies in scheduled, sharded batch runs, sized to each agency's rate limit. 92.section: Decision: queue submissions per agency, in Postgres
92.text: Problem Filing is a stampede. On a peak day about 1.7 million returns arrive, about 100 a second in the busiest hour (see Capacity Estimates ). Each agency accepts only so many a second, and agencies slow down or go offline at exactly these times. Without a queue: A rush passes straight through. Adding processor replicas to keep up adds load on the agency instead. Failures retry together. Returns that fail at the same moment all come back at the same moment, and hit a struggling agency again. One agency blocks the others. In a single queue, the IRS being down holds up California and New York. A failing return blocks the queue. If the oldest returns keep failing, they are picked first every time. Options considered Option For Against Send to the agency while the taxpayer waits Simplest; the taxpayer sees the agency's answer at once Agency slowness and outages become our outage, exactly at the deadline. Rejected. A message broker (SQS, Kafka, RabbitMQ) with a queue per agency Built-in delays and dead-letter queues; scales far past Postgres; the usual choice at very large scale The return and its message are written to two systems, so we'd need an outbox to keep them in step. Another system to run, secure, and monitor. Rate limits and circuit breakers still have to be built on top. A queue per agency in the returns table (chosen) The return and its place in the queue commit together, so none is lost or sent twice. No new infrastructure. Queue depth is one SQL query. Queue traffic shares the database with everything else. Needs care with indexes and row locks. How the queue works Mechanism What it prevents One queue per agency, drained separately each tick One agency's outage or backlog holding up another's Demo A token bucket per agency in agency_queues , shared by every replica ( SUBMIT_RPS ) More processors meaning more load on the agency Demo Claims with a short lease and FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED Two replicas sending the same return; a crashed replica losing one Demo Each failed return waits its own backoff: up to 2s, 4s, 8s… capped at 10 minutes, with full jitter Retry storms, and failing returns blocking the ones behind them Demo A circuit breaker per agency: 5 agency-side failures in a row stop sending for 30 seconds, then one probe decides Hammering an agency that is down, and wasting the batch on it Demo A return rejected for itself (a 4xx) retries on its own schedule without tripping the breaker One bad return shutting off an agency for everyone Demo Alerts on the age of the oldest queued return, and on an open breaker A backlog no one notices (see Monitoring & Alerting ) Planned Returns rejected repeatedly move to a review queue for support A return retrying forever without anyone knowing Planned Tested with two processor replicas, SUBMIT_RPS=1 , and 40 returns filed at once, with the New York agency down. Federal and California went out at one a second each across both replicas. New York's breaker opened after five failures without slowing the others, and its returns went out within seconds of the agency coming back. Settings Variable Default Meaning SUBMIT_RPS 10 Transmissions a second to each agency, across all processor replicas. Set from the agency's published limit, less what batch runs use. PROCESSOR_INTERVAL_MS 2000 How often each replica checks the queues Revisit when Queue writes and claims become a noticeable share of database load at peak. Other consumers need submission events, such as notifications or analytics. A broker fed from an outbox table becomes worth its cost. The service runs in more than one region.

93.text: Keep the status of every in-flight return current by asking the tax agencies in scheduled batches, instead of on every customer request.

94.text: The agencies own refund status: the IRS for federal returns, and each state's revenue agency for state returns. We can only learn it by asking them. Three facts make batching the right fit: Agency data changes slowly. The IRS updates refund status about once a day, overnight. Asking it 50 times a day about the same return returns the same answer 49 times. Customer traffic is spiky; agency capacity isn't. Reads peak at ~1,000 a second on refund-release mornings (see Capacity Estimates ). Passing those through would exceed agency rate limits exactly when customers care most. Agencies offer bulk lookups. One request can carry up to 100 submission IDs, so a batch costs 1% of the requests that one-at-a-time lookups would. Customers read status from our database, which batch runs keep current on our schedule and within each agency's limits.

95.text: Customer path: always reads our data Taxpayer Portal → API Reads stored status → Postgres tax_returns, history Filing: seconds after submission Processor Duplicate screening (pgvector) → Agency e-file IRS, state FTBs → Postgres submission ID, first check due Status sync: scheduled runs throughout the day Scheduler CronJob per agency → Batch shards Claim due returns, 100 per chunk → Agency status Bulk lookup, rate-limited → Postgres status, next check File. The API stores the return as Received . Within seconds the processor screens it for near-duplicates, then transmits it to the agency and stores the submission ID. The return is now Processing and due for its first check. Sync. A scheduler starts a run for each agency several times a day. The run's shards claim due returns in chunks of 100, call the agency's bulk status endpoint, and store each answer along with the next time that return should be checked. Read. The portal shows the stored status, the history, and when we last checked with the agency.

96.text: Customer reads never wait on, or add load to, an agency. Each agency gets its own schedule, rate limit, and credentials. Runs scale out by adding shards; shards never check the same return. A failed chunk or run is retried by the next run with no manual cleanup. Every run is recorded in batch_runs with its trace ID, so any run can be opened in Jaeger.

100.text: Each agency has its own schedule, set just after its own update cycle so a run sees fresh data. For example: Agency Updates Runs (Eastern time) IRS Once a day, overnight 05:00 main run; 11:00, 16:00, 21:00 catch-up runs for new transmissions and retries State agencies Varies: daily to several times a day Set per agency from its published update times and rate limit Runs for the same agency never overlap ( concurrencyPolicy: Forbid ). 101.text: Every return has a next_check_at . A run checks only returns that were due when it started, and each answer sets the next due time: Status after a check Next check Why Just transmitted Next run Confirm the agency has it Processing Next agency update cycle Nothing changes between updates Approved, payment date ahead On the payment date Nothing else changes before then Approved, payment date today or past Next update cycle Watch for Sent Sent, Accepted Never Final status (an operator can force a recheck) Agency needs more information Next update cycle The agency resolves it when the taxpayer responds Held by our duplicate screening Never (until released) Not transmitted yet Agency didn't recognise it, or the check failed Next run Try again Up to 10% random jitter is added to each due time, so millions of returns filed on the same day don't all come due in the same second. This policy is what brings agency lookups from ~140M to ~50M on a peak day (see Capacity Estimates ).

102.text: A run claims the most overdue returns first ( ORDER BY next_check_at ). If a run can't finish within its window, the oldest checks are done and the remainder rolls into the next run.

104.text: Splitting a run across workers, and sizing it for 40 million customers.

105.text: A run is split into shards by a hash of the return ID: shard i of N only claims returns where hash(id) mod N = i . On Kubernetes each run is an Indexed Job, and each pod reads its shard number from JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX . kubernetes/batch.yaml (excerpt) kind: CronJob spec: schedule: "0 5,11,16,21 * * *" # demo: every minute concurrencyPolicy: Forbid jobTemplate: spec: completionMode: Indexed completions: 8 # shards parallelism: 8 template: spec: containers: - args: ["batch-run", "federal"] env: - { name: BATCH_SHARDS, value: "8" } Copy

106.text: Within a shard, several workers claim chunks of up to 100 due returns at a time. A claim sets a short lease in the same statement that selects the rows: Claim the next chunk UPDATE tax_returns SET lease_until = now() + interval '2 minutes' WHERE id IN ( SELECT id FROM tax_returns WHERE jurisdiction = $1 AND status IN ('processing', 'approved') AND next_check_at <= $run_started_at AND (lease_until IS NULL OR lease_until < now()) AND mod(abs(hashtext(id::text)), $shards) = $shard ORDER BY next_check_at LIMIT 100 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) RETURNING id, agency_submission_id, status; Copy SKIP LOCKED means concurrent workers take different rows instead of waiting on each other. The lease keeps a claimed return out of other workers' hands while its agency call is in flight, without holding a database transaction open during the network call. A partial index on (jurisdiction, next_check_at) , covering only in-flight returns, keeps the query fast however many settled returns pile up. Results for a chunk are written in one transaction: the new status, a history entry for anything that changed, and the next due time.

107.text: From Capacity Estimates : a peak-day IRS run checks ~7.5M returns, 75,000 bulk requests. Three limits decide how many shards it needs: Limit Example Effect Agency rate limit 25 requests/s 75,000 ÷ 25 = 50 minutes minimum, however many shards Agency latency ~300 ms per bulk request 25 req/s × 0.3 s ≈ 8 requests in flight → 8 workers in total Database writes ~2,500 row updates/s Comfortable for one primary with 100-row transactions So the IRS run uses 2 shards × 4 workers, each shard limited to half the agency's rate. Smaller state agencies need one shard. The rate limit is shared: each process gets AGENCY_RPS ÷ BATCH_SHARDS .

109.text: Bulk status calls, credentials, rate limits, and retries. No agency offers this API today. E-file providers learn whether a return was accepted or rejected through the IRS Modernized e-File (MeF) acknowledgment system, which states also use. Refund status after acceptance is only available to taxpayers themselves, through the IRS "Where's My Refund?" tool and each state's equivalent. This design assumes a partner status feed with the shape below; the demo's mock agencies provide it, plus operator controls for the admin console .

110.text: Each agency client speaks two operations, behind one adapter per agency: Call Used by Purpose POST /v1/returns Processor Transmit a return. Our return ID is the idempotency key; the response is the agency's submission ID. POST /v1/statuses/batch-get Batch runs Status for up to 100 submission IDs, with payment date and when the agency last changed each one. Whatever each agency eventually offers (a bulk feed, files dropped on a schedule, or acknowledgments only), an adapter per agency turns it into these two calls, so the batch system doesn't change when an agency is added. Agency statuses map to ours: Agency says We show received, processing Processing approved (with payment date) Approved sent (the refund as filed) Refund sent adjusted (a different refund, with the reason) Refund adjusted accepted (no refund) Accepted action required (agency needs more information) Action needed not found No change; checked again next run

111.text: Each agency issues its own credentials. Production uses mutual TLS plus an API credential per agency, stored in a secret manager and rotated. Only the processor and batch pods can reach agencies; network policies block everything else. Requests carry submission IDs and our return IDs only: no names, tax IDs, or bank details.

112.text: Every client waits on a token bucket before each request ( AGENCY_RPS , divided across shards). A 429 response's Retry-After is always honoured, so we slow down when the agency asks even if our own limit would allow more.

113.text: Retried: network errors, 429 , and 5xx , up to 4 attempts with exponential backoff (100 ms, 200 ms, 400 ms, plus jitter) or Retry-After , whichever is longer. Not retried: other 4xx responses, which mean the request itself is wrong. Circuit breaker: after 5 failed chunks a run stops early instead of hammering an agency that is clearly down. See Failure Handling . The mock agencies fail 5% of status calls on purpose, so every demo run exercises retries. In Jaeger they show up as a 503 span followed by a successful retry in the same trace. Previous Sharding & Scale Next Failure Handling

Last known status, with an older "last checked" time Agency down After 5 failed chunks the circuit opens and the run stops. Each later run tries again. Same as above Worker pod crashes mid-run Leases on its chunks expire after BATCH_LEASE_SECONDS . The Job retries the pod ( backoffLimit ). Nothing Agency answers out of order, or omits IDs Results are matched by submission ID; omitted ones are released and checked next run. Nothing Transmission fails The return stays Received and is retried after a backoff with jitter. If the agency itself keeps failing, its circuit breaker pauses sending (see API Gateway ). "We'll send your return shortly"

115.text: Status checks are reads; asking twice changes nothing at the agency. Storing a result is idempotent: a status only produces a history entry when it differs from the stored one. Transmission uses our return ID as the idempotency key, so a retried submit doesn't file twice.

116.text: Every run writes a batch_runs row: status, returns checked, status changes, failed chunks, and trace ID. Alert when a run ends failed or partial twice in a row, or when any in-flight return hasn't been checked for more than a day: Returns overdue for a check SELECT jurisdiction, count(*) FROM tax_returns WHERE status IN ('processing', 'approved') AND next_check_at < now() - interval '24 hours' GROUP BY jurisdiction; Copy To investigate a run, copy its trace_id into Jaeger's search. See Distributed Tracing .

117.text: After an agency outage, run a catch-up batch without waiting for the schedule: kubectl -n tax-refund create job --from=cronjob/batch-federal batch-federal-manual Copy Previous Agency Integration

118.text: Until an agency sets a payment date, we estimate when the refund will be available. The strongest signal is the return itself. Phase 1 learns from which tax forms were filed, and how many of each. Phase 2 adds how big the figures on those forms are relative to the taxpayer's income. Phase 1: form types Phase 2: amounts relative to income The model sees A count of each form and schedule, plus timing, channel, and agency load Everything in Phase 1, plus each key figure as a share of income, in bands It can tell A return with Schedule C takes longer than one without A $2,000 deduction on $300,000 of income is routine; the same deduction on $25,000 is not Ships Season 2, shadowed against Season 1 outcomes first Once it beats Phase 1 in backtests, overall and in every income band

119.section: Why forms are the right signal
119.text: Complexity drives processing time. A return with one W-2 is matched and paid quickly. Add self-employment income, marketplace health coverage, or education credits, and there's more to reconcile and a better chance of review. Some forms trigger known holds. Refunds claiming the EITC or ACTC can't be issued before mid-February, and an injured spouse allocation adds weeks. The forms say so up front. We know the forms exactly. We prepared the return, so its composition is a fact, not a guess, and it's available the moment the return is filed. It explains the off season. Extension filers skew toward complex returns. A model that sees the forms doesn't need to treat October as a special case. See Extension Deadline .

120.text: For each return at each agency: the number of days from the agency accepting it until the refund is available, as a range (the 10th, 50th, and 90th percentiles). The estimate is refreshed whenever the status changes, given how long the return has already waited. It is replaced by the agency's own date as soon as there is one, and never shown once the refund has been sent.

121.text: Two survival algorithms, trained per agency on the same features in both phases. Both learn from returns that haven't been paid yet ("at least 30 days so far"), so estimates aren't biased toward the fast ones that finished first. Gradient-boosted survival Random survival forest Role Serves the estimates Checks them: an independent second model on the same data How XGBoost with the accelerated failure time objective: boosted trees predict the distribution of days until payment Many survival trees on random samples of returns and features, averaged into a full survival curve for each return Strengths Handles sparse form counts, finds interactions on its own (the EITC with an early filing date, a ratio with an income band), scores tens of millions of returns quickly, and explains itself with SHAP Assumes nothing about the shape of the distribution, so it catches ranges the boosted model gets wrong when real waits don't fit its assumed shape Watch for Assumes a distribution shape (normal, logistic, or extreme value), so its ranges need checking Slower to train and score, and large; it runs in the batch sync, never on a request In Phase 2 Monotone constraints on the ratio bands, so a larger ratio can never shorten an estimate No monotone constraints, which makes it a useful check on whether the constraints fit the data When they disagree. For each segment, if the forest's range differs from the boosted model's by more than a set margin, the estimate shows the wider of the two, and the segment is flagged for the next retraining review. Erring wide keeps the promise honest: refunds should land inside the range. Known rules sit on top. The estimate never falls before the EITC/ACTC release date, and an agency-set payment date always wins. A simple baseline first. Kaplan-Meier curves per form-family segment come before either model. They're the bar both models have to beat, the fallback if both are unavailable, and what the demo would build first.

122.text: Labels come from status history: the time from acceptance to "refund sent" or "refund adjusted" in return_events . Returns still waiting are kept as censored. Backtest by season: train on last season, test on this one, so the model is judged on data it couldn't have seen. Measure the error of the middle estimate, and how often the refund lands inside the range. About 80% should land between the 10th and 90th percentiles. Check both overall and per segment: each form family, each held credit, each filing month including October, and each refund size band, so complex or low-income returns aren't systematically wrong. Phase 2 adds each income band to the list. Phase 2 replaces Phase 1 only when it wins the same backtest on the same seasons, overall and in every segment, and then runs in shadow beside it before serving. Retrain weekly in season, run new versions in shadow before they serve, and keep every version in the registry for rollback.

123.text: Per-feature contributions (for example SHAP values) show which forms moved an estimate. Support agents see them directly: "Schedule C and Form 8962 add about a week." Taxpayers see a plain phrase, like "Returns with self-employment income usually take longer," never a suggestion that the agency is reviewing them.

124.text: Training uses only returns whose taxpayer consented under §7216, exported without identifiers to a separate ML environment, as shown in the High-Level Design . Form counts and bucketed amounts can still single someone out if the combination is rare enough. Any combination shared by fewer than 50 returns is rolled up to its form families before training. Inference payloads, logs, and traces carry the model version and a return token, never the features. If the model is slow, unavailable, or unsure, the status page falls back to the agency's published guidance, such as "most refunds within 21 days," and never waits on the model. Demo status: not built yet. Demo returns record only the main form and a few lines (wages, withholding, interest, itemized deductions, and dependents), so a demo Phase 1 model would start from a small form vocabulary derived from those. They already hold enough for one Phase 2 ratio: itemized deductions over wages and interest.

125.text: The first model knows what kind of return it is, not what's in it: which forms and schedules were filed, and how many of each. That alone separates a one-W-2 return from one with self-employment income, education credits, or a held EITC refund. It ships in Season 2, shadowed against Season 1 outcomes first.

A trained model learns them from how long similar returns actually took.

127.text: Group Features Why Form composition A count of each form and schedule in a fixed vocabulary: about 150 federal forms, plus each state's own. Anything outside it counts as "other". The core signal. Counts, never contents. Form families Totals for business, investment, credits, international, and information returns, and the number of distinct schedules Rare forms borrow strength from common ones in the same family. Held credits EITC and ACTC flags, and days until the mid-February release Encodes a legal hold the model shouldn't have to rediscover. Refund size The refund in bands, such as under $1,000 or $1,000 to $5,000 Large refunds are processed differently. Never the exact amount. Timing and channel Agency, week of the season, days since acceptance, e-file or paper, direct deposit or check The same return takes longer in April than in January. Agency load Each agency's median processing time for returns accepted in the same week Captures backlogs as they build. Never used: names, tax IDs, addresses or ZIP codes, employers, payers, bank details, and exact amounts. Prior-year history is used only if the taxpayer consented to it. What Phase 1 can't see is whether a figure is unusual for the person who filed it. Phase 2 adds that.

128.text: Phase 1 treats every Schedule A alike. Agencies don't: their screening compares each figure with what's normal for a return at that income. A deduction that's small next to a large income draws no more scrutiny than not having it, while the same deduction on a modest income stands out and is more likely to be reviewed. Phase 2 gives the model that context, so its estimate moves only when a figure is unusual for the person who filed it.

129.text: Figure on the return Charitable gifts ( Schedule A ) All itemized deductions ( Schedule A ) Business loss ( Schedule C ) Rental loss ( Schedule E ) Amount: $12,000 Total income: $60,000 Illustrative effect, on top of the form-type estimate +6 days Charitable gifts are 20% of income: over 20% . Gifts that are large for the income are compared against what similar filers give. The same $12,000 at other incomes $40,000 income · 30% +6d $100,000 income · 12% +3d $250,000 income · 4.8% +1d $500,000 income · 2.4% +0d Features Phase 2 adds income_band= 50k_100k charity /income= over_20 The bands and days are made up to show the idea. The model sees only the bands, never the amounts or the income, and learns from past returns how much each band actually adds.

130.text: Phase 2 keeps every Phase 1 feature and adds these, each in bands: Ratio Measured as Why it matters Deductions to income Total itemized deductions, and charitable gifts on their own, over total income Large deductions for the income are compared against similar filers. Losses to income Schedule C business losses and Schedule E rental losses over income from other sources Losses that wipe out other income are a common review trigger. Credits to tax Each refundable credit over the tax before credits, and the EITC over earned income Credits that exceed the tax by a wide margin get extra verification. Unmatched income share Income with no matching W-2 or 1099 (mostly self-employment) over total income Income the agency can't match against payer records takes longer to verify. Withholding to tax Tax withheld and paid over the tax owed, which sets the size of the refund relative to the return A refund out of proportion to the income is checked before it's paid. Income band Total income in bands, such as $50,000 to $100,000 Lets the model learn what's normal at each income, instead of one rule for everyone.

131.text: Bands, never amounts. Ratios and income are computed inside production and leave only as bands, like "3–10%" or "$50,000 to $100,000". The 50-return rollup in Privacy applies to the new combinations too, which matters more now that they're finer. No help gaming the agency. Taxpayers see the same plain wording as in Phase 1, such as "Returns like yours usually take a little longer." We never say which figure moved the estimate, so the estimate can't be used to tune deductions until they stop looking unusual. Support agents see the form families involved, not the ratios. Fair across incomes. Ratios run higher at low incomes by nature: the EITC is large relative to income by design. The model has to be checked per income band, so low-income returns aren't told to wait longer than they really do, and Phase 2 ships only if no band gets worse than in Phase 1. Prediction only. Like Phase 1, Phase 2 only estimates. It never changes how or when a return is filed, held, or checked.

132.text: Phase 1 has served at least one season and its ranges are calibrated, so there's a fair baseline to beat. Phase 2 wins the same season backtest, overall and in every segment, including each income band. It then runs in shadow beside Phase 1 before it serves anyone, and Phase 1 stays in the registry for rollback. Until then, Phase 1 serves alone. The demo's returns already hold enough for one Phase 2 ratio: itemized deductions over wages and interest.

133.text: A customer's account holds tax IDs, income, and bank details behind one sign-in. Security is the first design constraint for this service: every other decision is checked against it.

134.text: Account takeover pays. A taken-over account reveals income, filing details, and when a refund will land, which is everything a fraudster needs to phish the taxpayer or redirect future refunds. Refund fraud is organized. Rings file templated returns under stolen identities, route the refunds into a few bank accounts, and track them with the same status pages honest filers use. Attackers peak when we do. Credential stuffing and phishing surge in filing season, exactly when traffic is highest and there's pressure to relax controls to keep up. Trust is the product. One incident during filing season would push taxpayers back to the phone lines this service exists to relieve. The service must never tell anyone anything about a taxpayer unless they have proven they are that taxpayer, or are staff with a recorded reason to look.

135.text: Asset Why it matters Credentials and sessions The key to everything else in the account. Return figures Income, filing status, dependents, and the refund or balance due. Identifiers Tax IDs and bank accounts. We keep only the last 4 digits, plus a keyed fingerprint of the bank account. Refund status and dates Tell an attacker when money moves, which helps them time phishing and interception. Staff capabilities Admins can change what agencies report in the demo, and support staff can see any account. Training data Planned Status history for the refund-time model, which must never lead back to a person.

136.text: Controls are placed where data crosses from one level of trust to another: Internet → portal The only way in. TLS, security headers, bot and rate controls, request size limits. Portal → API Every request is authenticated by session, and authorized against the signed-in user. Services → Postgres Only pods labeled as database clients can connect; data at rest is encrypted. Workers → agencies Per-agency credentials, separate keys for admin actions, network policy allowlists. Production → ML environment Only consented, pseudonymized, coarse features cross, under a key that stays in production.

137.text: Prove it, then least access Strong sign-in once, then every query is scoped to that user's own returns. No oracle responses A failed sign-in looks and takes the same whether the email exists, the password is wrong, or the account is locked. Least data Never store what we can avoid: last 4 digits instead of full numbers, fingerprints instead of accounts. Read-only toward money Nothing here can change a refund amount or bank account, so compromising it can't redirect a refund. Zero trust inside Ingress is denied by default, and each service reaches only what it needs, with its own credentials. Assume breach Audit staff actions, keep sessions revocable in one step, and practice the response before it's needed.

146.text: Who would attack a tax refund service, what each wants, how they'd go about it here, and what stops them. Refunds are money and returns are identity, so this service draws more than its share of attackers, mostly in the same weeks taxpayers need it most.

The two highest are certain to happen at scale every season.

148.text: Credential stuffers Wants Working sign-ins, to resell or to use themselves. Tax accounts are valuable because they lead to refunds and identity data. Here, they'd Replay passwords leaked from other sites against our sign-in, spread across botnets and residential proxies so each address makes only a few attempts. Stopped by Per-IP, per-account, and per-password limits, and lockout an attacker can't turn against the owner Edge bot defense and breached-password checks Passkeys and second factors, so a password alone opens nothing We notice Failure rates and lockouts spiking, many accounts failing from few sources, and success rates that are oddly low for real people. Refund fraud rings Wants Refunds paid to accounts they control, under stolen identities, filed before the real taxpayer files. Here, they'd File templated returns early in the season, route many refunds to the same few bank accounts, and use the status service to see which filings got through. Stopped by Duplicate screening on bank fingerprints and near-identical figures, holding matches before they're sent Nothing in this service can change a refund amount or bank account Identity proofing before a return is filed We notice Many returns into one bank fingerprint, filing velocity per device or network, and accounts that check status unusually often. Phishers and impersonators Wants Credentials and bank details, taken on sites and channels they control. Here, they'd Lookalike domains and "there's a problem with your refund" emails and texts, timed to refund release dates and the April deadline. Stopped by Notifications that say only that something changed, with no links asking for anything, so ours can't be used as a template Passkeys, which can't be phished onto a lookalike site We notice Brand monitoring for lookalike domains (taken down quickly), DMARC reports of spoofed mail, and support calls about messages we didn't send. Someone close to the taxpayer Wants An ex-partner, a family member, or a housemate who wants to see the refund amount, where it's going, or where the taxpayer now lives, or to control the money. Here, they'd They know the taxpayer's tax ID, date of birth, and history, which defeats knowledge-based questions, and they may have used the taxpayer's devices. Stopped by No knowledge-based questions anywhere; passkeys and second factors instead Alerts for new devices, a list of active sessions, and sign out everywhere Support sees a return only when the taxpayer shares it from inside their own account We notice Sign-ins from a new device in an unusual pattern, and recovery attempts the owner didn't start. Support is trained to recognize callers who aren't the taxpayer. Insiders Wants Usually curiosity. Sometimes money: selling records, or helping a fraud ring by releasing held returns. Here, they'd Misuse legitimate support or admin access, often looking up people they know or browsing in bulk. Stopped by Support sees a return only while its taxpayer shares it, 5 minutes at a time; every view audited Two people to release a held return No person can decrypt return figures in production We notice Views without a case, out of hours, or in bulk; searches for names rather than case work; releases clustered on one admin. Dishonest or compromised preparers Wants Their clients' refunds, or their clients' data, or an attacker who has taken over the preparer's account wants the same. Here, they'd Use delegated access to many clients at once, sometimes from a firm whose own security is weak. Stopped by Verified PTIN and EFIN, client grants per taxpayer that the taxpayer can revoke, and MFA for preparers We notice A preparer touching far more clients than usual, or from new locations; clients revoking grants. Bulk data thieves and ransomware crews Wants The whole database to sell, or the service held hostage when downtime costs the most. Here, they'd Exploit a vulnerability, steal cloud or database credentials, or move sideways from another compromised system. Stopped by Minimal data: last 4 digits only, no full bank numbers, figures encrypted per taxpayer Workload identity, deny-by-default networking, and per-service credentials Keys in a separate account, and backups that ransomware can't reach We notice Unusual KMS decrypt volume, large reads or exports, new egress destinations, and access from unexpected identities. Supply-chain attackers Wants Code running inside the service, through a dependency, a base image, or the build. Here, they'd Publish a malicious package version, compromise a maintainer, or steal the credentials that deploy. Stopped by Pinned and reviewed dependencies, signed images built in isolated CI, and deploy credentials that can't be used outside the pipeline We notice Unexpected dependency changes in review, images without valid signatures blocked at deploy, and new outbound connections from pods. Nation-state actors Wants Data on millions of people for intelligence, taken quietly and kept for years. Here, they'd Patient, skilled intrusion: zero-days, supply chains, and long dwell time. Stopped by We don't claim to defeat them. The same controls raise the cost, minimal data limits what there is to take, and monitoring shortens how long they go unseen. We notice The same detection as above, plus threat intelligence shared through industry groups, the IRS, and government partners. Opportunistic scanners Wants Any easy way in: a known vulnerability, an exposed admin page, a default password. Here, they'd Automated scans of the whole internet. Stopped by Patching on a schedule, one public entry point, no exposed admin surfaces, and an edge firewall We notice Edge logs. Mostly noise, which is the point: they find nothing.

156.text: The two attacks on sign-in that matter most in filing season: finding out who has an account, and trying leaked passwords against them at scale.

The list feeds targeted phishing. Credential stuffing. Replay email and password pairs leaked from other sites, spread across residential proxies so each address only tries a few. Password spraying. 176.text: Identity work answers two questions that are easy to blur. Proofing asks, once, whether the person creating or claiming an account is the real taxpayer. Authentication asks, every time, whether the person signing in is the same one who was proofed. Most account takeovers exploit the seams between them: a weak recovery flow, a phone number changed without checks, or a sign-in that never needed proofing at all. We follow NIST SP 800-63-4 vocabulary: an identity assurance level (IAL) for proofing and an authentication assurance level (AAL) for sign-in. The target is IAL2 and AAL2 for any account that can see refund details, with AAL3-style hardware keys for staff.

223.text: Token buckets in a shared store. Each key (an IP, an account, a session) has a bucket in Redis, updated atomically, so every replica sees the same count. A bucket allows short bursts, like a page loading several things at once, while capping the sustained rate. The real client address. Per-IP limits use the address behind our own proxies, reading X-Forwarded-For from the right through the trusted ones only, so a client can't pick a fresh address for each attempt. See Enumeration & Credential Stuffing . If the shared store is down, each pod falls back to its own in-memory limits at a fraction of the shared limit. Protection gets coarser, but never switches off, and the status page keeps working. That's the trade the availability requirements ask for. Edge first. The edge drops floods before they reach us, so the application limits only see traffic that's already been filtered, and attacks don't spend our capacity.

224.text: Campuses, offices, and mobile carriers put thousands of people behind one IP address, and filing deadlines bring them all at once. Per-IP limits alone would block them together. So: Planned A device that has signed in successfully before carries a signed device cookie, and is counted on its own instead of with its whole network. Planned Known carrier and campus ranges get higher per-IP limits, and lean on the per-account and per-password limits instead. Planned Past a limit, a shared address gets a challenge before a block, so a person can still get through. See Bot Defense .

225.text: A hard lock after five failures stops guessing, but anyone who knows an email can lock its owner out on the busiest day of the year. The design escalates instead: Failures 1–3 Nothing visible. The count resets on a successful sign-in, and decays after 24 hours. Failures 4–5 Each attempt waits a little longer (1, then 2 seconds), and a challenge appears for unrecognized devices. After 5 Unrecognized devices are locked out for 15 minutes. Devices that signed in before can still sign in, with a second factor. The attacker is stopped; the owner isn't. Tell the owner The owner gets a notice that someone tried to sign in, telling them to sign in directly and change their password. It contains no link, so it can't be imitated by a phishing message. Unlock Waiting out the 15 minutes, resetting the password, or signing in with a second factor on a recognized device. Through all of it, the response to a failed sign-in is the same message, in the same time, whether the email exists, the password is wrong, or the account is locked.

228.text: Telling automated attacks from taxpayers, and making the attacks too slow and expensive to pay off, while nearly every real taxpayer never notices anything at all.

229.text: Layers, not a wall. No single signal is reliable. The edge, risk scoring, rate limits, and fraud checks each catch what the others miss. Invisible first. Signals and scoring cost a taxpayer nothing. Puzzles are the last resort, not the default. Friction in proportion to risk. A known device signing in sees nothing; a new device from a botnet range sees a challenge. Everyone can get through. Every challenge has an accessible path. Shutting out people who use assistive technology would fail the people this service is for. On through the peak. Bot traffic hides in the April rush, so defenses are sized for it and never switched off to keep up. What bots try against this service is listed in Bots & Automated Abuse . This page is how we stop them.

230.text: Edge filter The CDN and web application firewall drop floods, known-bad networks, and malformed requests before they reach us. Risk score Bot management scores each sign-in, sign-up, and recovery request on the signals below, and passes the score to the app. Response The score picks a step on the response ladder: allow, watch, slow, challenge, or block. App limits Rate limits and lockout catch what scoring misses, counted per IP, per account, and per password. See Rate Limiting & Lockout . Business checks Duplicate screening and fraud scoring catch automated filing that looked human all the way in.

231.text: Signal Examples Catches Privacy Network IP reputation, data-center and hosting ranges, known proxies and anonymizers Cheap botnets and rented servers Uses the address we already log; no new data Client fingerprint TLS and HTTP/2 handshake fingerprints, header order, whether the browser environment is real Scripts pretending to be browsers A hash of how the client connects, not who the person is Behavior Typing rhythm, pointer and touch movement, time to fill a form, the path through the pages Automation that is fast, uniform, or skips steps Summarized into a score in the browser session; raw movements aren't kept Velocity Attempts per account, device, network, and password, over minutes and days Stuffing, spraying, and bulk filing spread thin Counters with short expiries Device history A signed cookie on devices that signed in successfully before Lets known devices through with less friction A random ID, not a fingerprint; cleared by the user at will Credential intelligence Passwords known from breaches, checked by a k-anonymity range query Stuffing with leaked lists The password never leaves us; only a short hash prefix is sent Tripwires Hidden form fields, decoy endpoints, and canary accounts Bots that fill or crawl everything No personal data involved Signals are used only to tell people from bots: never for marketing, never sold, kept 90 days at most, and named in the privacy notice.

232.text: Step When What happens Allow Low risk: most traffic, and every known device Nothing. The taxpayer never sees bot defense. Watch Slightly unusual Allowed, but tagged so later requests in the session are scored with that in mind. Slow Suspicious, or a burst Small added delays. Costs a person a second; costs a bot its throughput. Challenge Likely automated An invisible check first (proof-of-work or device attestation); an interactive, accessible one only if that fails. Block Clearly automated, or a tripwire hit Refused, with a generic response that doesn't say which signal tripped. Repeat sources may be slowed to a crawl instead of refused, which wastes their time.

233.text: Invisible checks first. A short proof-of-work, or a device attestation token from the browser or operating system, proves a real device without asking the person to do anything. Interactive only if those fail, and always with an accessible alternative. WCAG 2.2's accessible authentication criterion rules out puzzles that depend on memory or transcription without another way through. Passkeys skip the question. A passkey sign-in proves a real device and a real person in one step, so the more taxpayers use them, the fewer challenges anyone sees. Proof-of-work under attack. During a stuffing campaign, sign-in can require a small computation from every new device: a fraction of a second for one person, a real cost for millions of attempts.

235.text: Hidden fields. Form fields people can't see or reach. Anything that fills them is a bot. Decoy endpoints. Paths no page links to, listed nowhere a person would look. A hit is a crawler or a scanner, and its source is blocked. Canary accounts. Accounts that exist only to be watched. Any sign-in attempt means their credentials are circulating in a list, which tells us a campaign has started and which list it's using.

236.text: Under-attack mode. A pre-approved switch raises the challenge rate for new devices and turns on proof-of-work at sign-in. It's in the runbook, so on-call can turn it on in minutes without a deploy. If the bot-defense vendor fails, traffic passes through unscored rather than being blocked, so the status page stays up, and the application's own rate limits and lockout carry the load. That follows the order in Availability & Latency . Shared intelligence. Block lists and indicators are shared with the IRS, the states, and industry groups through the season, so a campaign seen elsewhere is blocked here before it starts.

248.text: Triage On-call assigns a severity. Anything involving taxpayer data goes to the security lead and privacy counsel. 249.text: The obligations that shape this design. This is an engineering summary, not legal advice; counsel confirms the specifics.

250.text: Rule What it means here IRC §7216 and its regulations Tax return information can't be used or disclosed beyond preparing the return without the taxpayer's consent. Using it to train the refund-time model needs explicit, separate opt-in consent. FTC Safeguards Rule (GLBA) A written security program with a responsible owner, risk assessments, MFA, encryption, regular testing, and notifying the FTC of qualifying breaches. IRS e-file and safeguarding guidance Publication 1345 rules for e-file providers, Publication 4557 safeguards, and reporting data theft to the IRS. State privacy and breach laws Rights to access and delete personal data (for example CCPA/CPRA), limits on sensitive data, and breach notification deadlines that vary by state. SOC 2 Type II Independent evidence, for partners and enterprise customers, that the controls on these pages operate over time.

251.text: We show a taxpayer only their own returns, and staff see them only with a recorded reason. Refund estimates are made for everyone; only taxpayers who opt in contribute to training, and they can withdraw. We never sell return information or use it for advertising. Taxpayers can see and export their data, and delete their account once retention rules allow. Notifications never include links that ask for credentials or bank details, so customers can tell them apart from phishing.

Pre-scaled, capacity reserved, and agency rate limits confirmed. On-call staffed, every paging alert has a runbook, and support is briefed. Change freeze announced, and feature flags in place for anything still risky.

277.text: Taxpayers who file for an extension have until October 15. That's a much smaller spike than April, but it lands in the off season, when the system is scaled down and fewer people are watching. Here's how big it is, and how we plan for it.

278.text: The IRS publishes cumulative filing-season statistics every week. Comparing the snapshot just after April 15 with the one just after October 15 shows how much arrives late: Individual returns By mid-April By mid-October Arrived after mid-April Returns received, 2024 139.1M (Apr 19) 161.5M (Oct 18) ~22.4M, 14% of the year Refunds issued, 2024 86.1M 103.2M ~17.1M, 17% of the year Returns received, 2025 140.6M (Apr 18) 163.6M (Oct 17) ~23.0M, 14% of the year Refunds issued, 2025 86.0M 102.1M ~16.1M, 16% of the year Returns received, 2026 140.2M (Apr 17) Not published yet ~4.8M in the first three weeks (145.0M by May 8), against ~5.2M in the same weeks of 2025 The share is steady at about 14% of returns, and 2026 is tracking 2025 so far. The IRS hasn't yet published an October snapshot for 2026. Not every late return is an extension: some are simply filed late, and some refunds are for returns filed earlier that took longer to process. The IRS doesn't publish a regular count of extension requests, but in 2019 it said it expected about 14.6 million.

279.text: About 5–6 million late federal returns. If our 40 million customers file like the country does, about 14% of their federal returns arrive after mid-April, many of them clustered in the weeks before October 15. Their refunds keep arriving through November and December. Capacity isn't the risk. Spread over six months, with one short spike, that's well under the April peak the system is already sized for. Capacity Estimates assumes about 10% of filings fall outside the main season; the IRS figures suggest closer to 14%, which is inside the margin of planning at twice the forecast. Timing is the risk. By October we've scaled down, lifted the change freeze, moved on-call to business hours, and may be shipping changes for next season.

280.section: Why it still needs a plan
280.text: The deadline moves. The IRS regularly postpones deadlines for federally declared disaster areas, sometimes by months, and some states set their own extension dates. October 15 is the usual date, not a constant. The tail overlaps the next season. Refunds for October filings arrive in November and December, and some state refunds later still. In January, the batch sync is still tracking last year's stragglers while the new season opens, so two tax years are in flight at once. Estimates are weakest here. Extension filers skew toward complex returns, such as self-employment and investment income, and most training data comes from peak season.

281.text: Planned A small readiness cycle in late September: scale up for the final two weeks, freeze changes from about October 10 to 17, and run in-season on-call that week. Planned Keep deadlines as per-jurisdiction settings that operations can change without a release, so a disaster postponement is a configuration change. Planned Keep checking a return until it reaches a final status, whatever the season. Partition data by tax year, and show a customer both their new return and any prior-year refund still in flight, rather than only the most recent one. Planned Measure the refund-time model on off-season filings separately. Where its ranges don't hold up, fall back to the agency's published guidance. Planned Alerts compare with the same week last season, so they neither go quiet nor get noisy just because October traffic is low.

285.text: Status Means Received We sent the return to the agency; it hasn't started processing. Processing The agency is validating and reviewing the return. 286.text: Uniform failures. An unknown email and a wrong password produce the same message, so a failed sign-in never confirms that an account exists. Constant response time. 311.text: Fixes for the problems you're most likely to hit. Pods stuck in ErrImageNeverPull or ImagePullBackOff The cluster can't see your local images. On Docker Desktop, make sure the context is docker-desktop . On other clusters, set K8S_LOAD as shown in Other Clusters . Pods stuck in Pending Usually not enough memory. Give Docker Desktop more under Settings → Resources, and see why with kubectl --context docker-desktop -n tax-refund describe pod <name> . make k8s-forward says the address is already in use Something else is using port 8090. Forward to another port instead: kubectl --context docker-desktop -n tax-refund port-forward svc/frontend 9090:80 . The portal stopped responding after a deploy The port-forward was attached to a pod that has been replaced. Stop it and run make k8s-forward again. Sign-in says to wait 15 minutes Five wrong passwords lock an account for 15 minutes. Wait it out, or start fresh with make k8s-delete and make k8s-deploy . Returns stay in Processing The batch runs aren't succeeding. Run make k8s-batch : if jobs show Failed , read a pod's logs with kubectl --context docker-desktop -n tax-refund logs -l app.kubernetes.io/name=batch --tail=50 . A run marked partial hit agency errors and will retry on the next run. A few failed batch jobs right after a deploy Runs that started during the rollout can fail; the next minute's run picks up their work. Kubernetes keeps the last three failed jobs for inspection. Jaeger shows no traces Traces arrive a few seconds after a span ends. Check the jaeger pod is running with make k8s-status . Jaeger keeps traces in memory, so they're gone after it restarts. 320.text: The IRS and the states don't offer an API for refund status. The demo's mock agencies stand in for them, and the admin console lets you decide what they say instead of waiting for their automatic timeline. That makes it easy to show any situation on demand: an approval, a refund sent as filed, an adjusted refund, or a request for more information.

321.text: Open the portal ( localhost:8090 on Kubernetes, localhost:8088 in Docker, localhost:5180 in dev mode) and sign in as admin@test.com with the password test . Admins go straight to the console at /admin .

322.text: The console lists every taxpayer who has sent in a return, newest activity first, with their federal and state returns underneath. Column Means Taxpayer sees The status in our database, the amount if the agency set one, and the latest message: exactly what the taxpayer's dashboard shows. Also when we last checked the agency and when we'll check next. Agency has (live) What the mock agency says right now, including any refund amount, balance due, payment date, and message, and whether that's its Automatic timeline or Set by admin .

323.text: Choose a status, fill in what it needs, and click Send to taxpayer . Status Details sent to the taxpayer Received, Processing Optional message Approved The refund as filed, with an expected payment date (required), optional message Refund sent The refund as filed, deposited on a date (required), optional message Refund adjusted A refund different from the claim, its deposit date, and why it changed (all required). Sending the amount as filed is refused: that's Refund sent. Accepted (returns with no refund) Balance due, optional message Action required A message saying what the agency needs (required) Send to taxpayer sets the status at the mock agency and immediately runs a status check for that one return, through the same code path as batch runs, so the taxpayer's dashboard updates right away. If that check can't run (say the agency mock is restarting), the return is left due and the next batch run delivers it.

324.text: Randomize appears for statuses with details, and fills them with a plausible agency decision. Edit anything before sending. Status What it picks Approved A payment date 5–21 days from today. Refund sent A deposit date 0–3 days ago. Refund adjusted 80–105% of the claim (never exactly the claim), with a matching reason (a math error, an offset for a past-due debt, an adjusted or newly found credit). Deposited 0–3 days ago. Accepted The balance as filed, up to 10% higher, with a reminder to pay by April 15. Action required One of several realistic requests: verify identity, send W-2 copies, confirm the bank account, document dependents, or resolve a duplicate return. The server enforces limits whatever the console sends: adjusted refunds between $1 and the larger of 150% of the claim or the claim plus $1,000; a balance due between $0 and the larger of twice the filed balance or $5,000 over it; messages of at most 500 characters, and at least 10 for Refund adjusted and Action required.

325.text: Resume automatic Removes your override, so the agency goes back to its automatic timeline for that return. Check now Checks the return with its agency right away. It also works on returns in a final status, which batch runs otherwise stop checking. Identity verified: release and send Shown for returns our duplicate screening held before they were sent. It records that identity was verified, and the processor sends the return to the agency without screening it again.

Choose Refund sent instead for a refund paid as filed. Both are final, so batch runs stop checking the return until you change it again. Open Jaeger and find the refund-api trace for PUT /api/admin/returns/…/agency-status : the call to the agency, then the batch.check_one sync that delivered it. Use a separate window for the admin. Sessions are cookies, so signing in as the admin in the same browser window signs the taxpayer out.

327.text: The console calls admin endpoints on our API, which only accept users with the admin role. Every action is written to audit_log with the admin's ID, and so is every search and every return an admin is shown ( admin_view_returns ). The page refreshes every 5 seconds, so a view is logged once per admin every 15 minutes rather than on every refresh. The API forwards status changes to the mock agency's operator endpoints, using a separate key ( AGENCY_ADMIN_KEY ) that only the admin endpoints use. In the demo every workload still loads it from the shared secret; see Service-to-Service Auth . The mock agency stores overrides in its own agency_mock schema. Our own tables are never edited directly: a status check reads the agency's new status, amount, and message and updates them, the same path a real change would take. Recent admin actions SELECT a.action, u.email, a.detail, a.created_at FROM audit_log a JOIN users u ON u.id = a.user_id WHERE a.action LIKE 'admin_%' ORDER BY a.id DESC LIMIT 20; Copy To check the whole flow from the command line, run scripts/admin-smoke-test.sh with the portal's address, for example scripts/admin-smoke-test.sh http://localhost:8088 . 353.text: Connect to Postgres and see what the system stores. psql postgres://taxrefund:taxrefund@localhost:5432/taxrefund Copy Table Holds users Accounts, password hashes, lockout state. Only the last 4 digits of the tax ID. tax_returns Each return, its calculation, status, and feature vector return_events Status history shown on the dashboard sessions Hashed session tokens and expiry times audit_log Sign-ins, failures, filings, and resets batch_runs One row per batch run and shard: outcome, counts, and trace ID

354.text: SELECT id, jurisdiction, status, returns_checked, status_changes, chunks_failed, trace_id FROM batch_runs ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 10; Copy Paste a trace_id into Jaeger's search box to open that run. Each in-flight return's last_checked_at and next_check_at show the schedule at work.

355.text: This query finds each return's closest return from another taxpayer, the same way the processor does: SELECT a.form, ua.email AS filed_by, ub.email AS closest_other_taxpayer, round((a.features <=> b.features)::numeric, 4) AS distance FROM tax_returns a JOIN users ua ON ua.id = a.user_id CROSS JOIN LATERAL ( SELECT r.user_id, r.features FROM tax_returns r WHERE r.user_id <> a.user_id AND r.jurisdiction = a.jurisdiction ORDER BY r.features <=> a.features LIMIT 1 ) b JOIN users ub ON ub.id = b.user_id; Copy A distance under SIMILARITY_THRESHOLD (default 0.02) is what sends a return to Action needed. 356.text: Where to make the changes you're most likely to need. Change the database schema Add a new file such as 002_add_column.sql to backend/internal/store/migrations/ . Migrations run in file-name order on the next backend start, each exactly once. Don't edit files that have already been applied. Add a demo user Add an entry to backend/internal/store/demo-users.json and restart the backend. Set "role": "admin" for another admin. For more than one state, give it "states" , each with a residency of resident , part_year , or nonresident (at most one resident), and a draft for each state's form. States with no income tax (FL, TX, WA) get no form or draft; "states": [] means federal only. Demo accounts are updated to match the file, including passwords, every time the backend starts. Change the tax math Edit backend/internal/tax/ and update tax_test.go . The portal shows whatever the server calculates. Change the portal Pages are in frontend/src/pages/ and the API client is frontend/src/api.js . Changes show up in the browser as soon as you save. Start with an empty database Run make reset-db . It wipes every table and re-seeds the demo accounts, while dev mode or the Docker stack keeps running. To clear just one tester's returns, use Reset demo returns in the portal. 358.text: Fixes for the problems you're most likely to hit. Port 5432 is already in use Another Postgres is running. Stop it, or use a different port for both Postgres and the backend: POSTGRES_PORT=55432 make dev-db , then run the backend with DATABASE_URL=postgres://taxrefund:taxrefund@localhost:55432/taxrefund?sslmode=disable . Port 5180 or 8080 is already in use An earlier make dev may still be running. Find it with lsof -nP -iTCP:5180 -sTCP:LISTEN and stop it. Sign-in fails with "Request failed (502)" or similar The backend isn't reachable. Check that curl localhost:8080/api/healthz answers, and look at the backend's output for errors. Returns stay in Received The processor isn't running, or can't reach the agency mocks. make dev-backend runs both; with taxrefund serve alone, nothing transmits. Returns stay in Processing Batch runs aren't happening or are failing. Look for batch run finished lines in the backend output, or query batch_runs . A partial run hit agency errors and retries next time. Port 4318 or 16686 is already in use Another Jaeger or OpenTelemetry Collector is running. Stop it, or point the backend at it with OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT . Sign-in says to wait 15 minutes Five wrong passwords lock an account for 15 minutes. Wait, or clear the lock in the database: UPDATE users SET failed_logins = 0, locked_until = NULL; Previous Configuration
